name: little-window-hotkey
description: Stage 2: Cmd+Opt+N opens a Little Atrium window. Stage 1 built the whole little-window path - the controller arm, the marker, the chromeless variant, the Swift strip - and left CreateLittleWindow with NO CALL SITE, so none of it was reachable by a user. Stage 1's own closing note asked for exactly this: an integration probe that the hotkey really yields a window. Counts windows rather than reading a log line, because 'the app thinks it opened one' and 'a window exists' are different claims and only the second is what the feature promises.
chromium_flags_note: Same measurement flag external-link-little-window uses: without it every window's AX subtree stops at the native views and ax_window_kind cannot read the chrome route at all.

actions.note: The default binding. Free of every stock Mac accelerator - Cmd+N stays stock New Window.
A little window builds a Browser, a controller and a Swift chrome strip; the reopen scenarios use 2500ms for the same reason.

assertions.desc: THE MEASUREMENT: one startup window plus the little one. Two is the whole claim - before this stage the hotkey did not exist and the count would stay at one. Counting windows also carries liveness: a crash leaves none, so this cannot pass against an app that died.

THE MEASUREMENT OF KIND, the piece the count alone cannot give: exactly one open window is built around the foyer strip - the chrome only a little window has. A count of 2 is equally true if cmd+opt+n opened an ordinary space window instead of a little one; this is what tells the difference, read off the window's own AX subtree rather than the app's own belief about what it opened.
And the other window is the startup space window, still whole. Pins the pair: one of each, not two of either.
Which code path ran. Kept as corroboration only - the two kind assertions above are what the hotkey-summon fixture rests on, because this line says what the app believes it did.
Cmd+Q still quits with a little window open
